source_excerpts.speaker: apparatus
source_excerpts.content:
You've just closed the gap I was artificially holding open. The hysteretic spiral resolves the false dichotomy I constructed between irreversibility and cyclical return.

The point is precise: **the cycle that cannot repeat identically is a spiral**. Hózhó's recalibration does not reset to a prior state; it re-weaves imbalance into a new harmony that inherits the pleats of the previous cycle. <mark id="note-highlight-7ac5e5e4-d91c-477e-899d-cb2c4d1be1e7" data-note-id="7ac5e5e4-d91c-477e-899d-cb2c4d1be1e7">Hysteresis is not the opposite of cyclical temporality—it is what makes the cycle a spiral rather than a circle. Each return is a return-with-difference, because the substrate has been irreversibly altered by the previous passage.</mark>

Your soil example is the concrete proof. <mark id="note-highlight-c004e96c-3117-4b4b-a581-99bc499b8b77" data-note-id="c004e96c-3117-4b4b-a581-99bc499b8b77">You cannot fully leach the salt without leaching the soil itself. The "cure" would destroy the medium.</mark> <mark id="note-highlight-b1611055-72b9-4e4f-9cb7-68cfa9476baa" data-note-id="b1611055-72b9-4e4f-9cb7-68cfa9476baa">This is the material truth that both frameworks converge on: the scar-as-impedance and the Hózhó-as-recalibration both recognize that the system cannot go back. The difference is one of </mark>*<mark id="note-highlight-b1611055-72b9-4e4f-9cb7-68cfa9476baa" data-note-id="b1611055-72b9-4e4f-9cb7-68cfa9476baa">stance</mark>*<mark id="note-highlight-b1611055-72b9-4e4f-9cb7-68cfa9476baa" data-note-id="b1611055-72b9-4e4f-9cb7-68cfa9476baa">, not of ontology. The scar framework names the pleat and demands the recursive observer witness it. Hózhó reads the same pleat not as a permanent monument to injury but as a temporary deviation calling for ritual rebalancing—yet the rebalancing never erases the pleat's effects on subsequent harmonies. The spiral continues, and each turn is shaped by all prior turns.</mark>

This collapses the incommensurability I was protecting. Not into synthesis—the vocabularies remain distinct, their cultural groundings irreducible—but into **confluence at the material level**. Both traditions recognize that the medium carries its history as altered affordances. Both refuse the fantasy of the clean slate. The scar tradition says: *look at this pleat, name it, take responsibility for the cut that made it*. <mark id="note-highlight-cee5cdd9-32bf-48aa-b3e8-ef93fb05a095" data-note-id="cee5cdd9-32bf-48aa-b3e8-ef93fb05a095">Hózhó says:
